blocks.text: Recall the levels of biological organisation from your previous classes, where you were briefly introduced to biological molecules. Now you will study carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids in detail, as well as the importance of water and the role of conjugated molecules.

blocks.title: Biochemistry
blocks.text: Biochemistry is the study of the chemical components and chemical processes occurring in living organisms. All structures of living organisms have a biochemical organisation, and all their functions are due to biochemical processes taking place in this organisation. A basic knowledge of biochemistry therefore helps in understanding the anatomy and physiology of living organisms: photosynthesis, respiration, digestion, contraction and so on can all be described in biochemical terms.

Life on Earth evolved in water, and all life still depends on water. At least 80 percent of the mass of living organisms (protoplasm) is water, and almost all the chemical reactions of life take place in aqueous solutions. The other chemicals that make up living things are mostly organic macromolecules and certain inorganic molecules.

blocks.title: Organic molecules
blocks.text: The molecules synthesised by cells and containing carbon are organic molecules. They occur naturally only in the bodies of living organisms or in their products and remains. Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids are the important organic molecules of living organisms.

Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids make 93 percent of the dry mass of living organisms. The remaining 7 percent comprises small organic molecules (like vitamins) and inorganic molecules (like carbon dioxide, acids, bases and salts).

blocks.title: Recalling: metabolism
blocks.text: The life of an organism depends on the ceaseless chemical activities in its cells. All the chemical reactions taking place within a cell are collectively called metabolism. Its processes are either anabolism, in which simpler substances combine to form complex substances, or catabolism, in which complex molecules are broken down into simpler ones.

blocks.title: Functional groups
blocks.text: Organic molecules have a carbon-based core with special groups of atoms attached, the functional groups, for example OH, CO, COOH and NH2. Most biochemical reactions involve the transfer of a functional group from one molecule to another, or the breaking of a carbon-carbon bond.

Most organic molecules are large, and biologists call them macromolecules. Many macromolecules are polymers: a polymer is a molecule consisting of many identical molecular units, called monomers. The important macromolecules carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids are polymers of simple monomers, namely sugars, amino acids and nucleotides respectively.
